clinicalPearls: An alpha-dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic POMT1 variants; POMT1 acts with POMT2 to initiate O-mannosylation of alpha-dystroglycan.
Represents the mild end of the POMT1 spectrum, whose severe end is Walker-Warburg syndrome with brain and eye malformation.
Childhood-onset proximal weakness, frequently accompanied by calf (and sometimes thigh or tongue) hypertrophy.
Cognitive impairment or microcephaly may occur even when brain imaging is relatively normal.
Creatine kinase is typically markedly elevated.
Muscle biopsy shows reduced glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan (for example with the IIH6 antibody) despite a preserved core protein.
Genetic testing distinguishes it from other dystroglycanopathies caused by FKRP, FKTN, POMT2 and POMGNT1.
reference.pathophysiology: Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R11 is an alpha-dystroglycanopathy caused by biallelic hypomorphic variants in POMT1 on chromosome 9q34.13, which encodes protein O-mannosyltransferase 1. Working in a complex with POMT2, this enzyme catalyses the first committed step of O-mannosyl glycan synthesis on alpha-dystroglycan; the resulting matriglycan is essential for high-affinity binding of alpha-dystroglycan to laminin and other extracellular-matrix ligands that anchor the sarcolemma. Severe null variants abolish glycosylation and produce lethal Walker-Warburg syndrome with cobblestone lissencephaly and eye malformation, whereas the milder residual-function variants underlying LGMD R11 permit partial glycosylation, giving a limb-girdle phenotype often accompanied by calf hypertrophy and cognitive impairment or microcephaly with relatively preserved brain structure. Muscle shows reduced immunolabelling of glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan despite a normally expressed core protein.
additionalDifferentials: Walker-Warburg syndrome and muscle-eye-brain disease (severe end of the spectrum)
Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy (calf hypertrophy with high creatine kinase)
additionalInvestigations: Next-generation sequencing gene panel or whole-exome sequencing covering POMT1 and other dystroglycanopathy genes
Muscle biopsy with glycosylated alpha-dystroglycan immunostaining
Brain MRI to exclude structural malformation
redFlags: Developmental regression or a new focal neurological deficit
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable; the limb-girdle end of the spectrum progresses more slowly than congenital forms, but the rate of motor progression and the degree of cognitive involvement strongly influence prognosis.
pitfalls: Markedly raised creatine kinase with calf hypertrophy can be mistaken for a dystrophinopathy.
A normal brain MRI does not exclude clinically significant cognitive involvement.
Reduced alpha-dystroglycan glycosylation is shared across dystroglycanopathies and is not gene-specific.
Milder cases may present later than expected and be misclassified.
management: Recognise there is no disease-specific pharmacotherapy and use physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain motor function and prevent contractures
Provide cognitive assessment with educational and developmental support for associated intellectual impairment or microcephaly
Undertake respiratory surveillance with non-invasive ventilation and cardiac monitoring, as dystroglycanopathies can involve heart and respiratory muscle
Arrange neuroimaging to exclude a structural brain malformation
Deliver multidisciplinary paediatric neuromuscular care and rehabilitation
Provide genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and family screening
